1.pericope_label: He came into his own city; and they brought to him a man sick of the palsy

schools.summary: Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson identify the city as Capernaum and fill the scene out from the parallels: four bearers, a crowded courtyard, scribes down from Jerusalem, and an eastern house whose awning-covered court explains the uncovered roof. Ellicott insists the Greek reports a pardon already granted, not a wish.

Gill supplies the four bearers from Mark; Calvin turns the seen faith into a general question of how far one profits by another's belief, extending grace to believers' children but insisting the paralytic must have believed himself, and reads the pardon as Christ beginning at the cause of the affliction.
Clarke reports the rabbinic maxim that no diseased person was healed until his sins were blotted out, grounding it in the psalm that joins forgiving iniquity to healing disease.

Henry reads the crossing as Christ taking the Gadarenes at their word, finding justice in the departure and patience in the absence of judgment, and notes that Gadara was among the first towns besieged when the Roman wars began.

Chrysostom distributes the towns, Bethlehem for birth, Nazareth for upbringing, Capernaum for continual dwelling, separates this paralytic from the man at the pool, and allows that the sick man had faith of his own.

Jerome dissents on the city, allowing Nazareth, and exclaims at the humility of addressing a despised cripple as son; Augustine harmonises by letting all Galilee be called Christ's city; Chrysologus marvels that another's faith healed a man within and without.

debates.question: Which city is called his own?

positions.view: Capernaum, his settled residence
possibly Nazareth, whence he was called a Nazarene
any town of Galilee, as the empire was called the Roman city
that of the bearers only
the sick man believed too, or he would not have been lowered

outliers.claim: the verse properly belongs to the preceding chapter
the Pharisees present from Jerusalem are one of the few traces of an unrecorded Jerusalem ministry

themes: And he entered into a ship, and passed over, and came into his own city.
And, behold, they brought to him a man sick of the palsy, lying on a bed: and Jesus seeing their faith said unto the sick of the palsy; Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee.

3.pericope_label: That ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins

schools.summary: Barnes grants the scribes reasoned correctly that none but God forgives sins; Ellicott hears an echo of the Jerusalem charge and lists what they failed to weigh; Robertson reads the narrator's aside inside the saying as evidence that the later Gospels used Mark; Ellicott and Barnes both handle the crowd's cry as a report of feeling rather than doctrine.

Gill treats the discernment of thoughts as proof of deity; Calvin faults the scribes for slandering in silence instead of asking, marks off Christ's granting of pardon from the declaring done by pastors, and finds the crowd's confession half right.
Clarke derives the word for blasphemy, counts three miracles in the episode, notes manuscripts reading feared for wondered, and observes that learning not held in dependence on God only blinds.
Chrysostom weighs the two sayings, holding that forgiving sin is the greater work but the visible cure the more evident, so the lesser miracle proves the greater.

Jerome says that in seeing their thoughts he shewed himself God, who alone knows the heart; the Gloss notes that the clause about knowing may belong to Christ or to the Evangelist, leaving the sentence unfinished either way.

debates.question: Who speaks the clause about knowing that the Son of man has authority?

positions.view: either Christ or the Evangelist; if Christ's, the sentence is left imperfect
the narrator interrupts the saying, as Mark does in the same place

debates.question: Did the crowd wonder or fear?

positions.view: the better manuscripts read feared

outliers.claim: the comma belongs after easier, making the words to say the start of the question

themes: And, behold, certain of the scribes said within themselves, This man blasphemeth.
And Jesus knowing their thoughts said, Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?
For whether is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and walk?
But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house.
And he arose, and departed to his house.
But when the multitudes saw it, they marvelled, and glorified God, which had given such power unto men.

9.pericope_label: He saith unto him, Follow me; and many publicans and sinners sat down with him

schools.summary: Barnes notes that Luke records the leaving of all which Matthew omits, reading humility in the silence; Ellicott proposes a new name superseding an old and takes the meal for a farewell feast; Robertson places the custom-house on the Damascus caravan route and explains the contempt for publicans by graft; Lightfoot puts him by the sea and relays a Talmudic tradition naming five disciples.

Gill supplies the great feast from Luke and reads Matthew's desire that his old companions hear Christ; Calvin makes the choice of a publican an example of undeserved goodness, thinks Levi was his ordinary name, and finds in his readiness the divine power of the word.

Clarke derives the name from a Syriac word for a gift and reflects on how much is lost by delaying obedience to a first call; Wesley supplies the feast from Mark and glosses the infamy of the tax-collectors.
Henry observes that Christ found him at work rather than idle, that Matthew was not seeking Christ but was spoken to first, and that unlike the fishermen he never returns to his old post.
Chrysostom asks why the call came so late and answers that Matthew was still hardened until many miracles had passed, and praises the evangelist for not disguising his former life.

Jerome explains that the other evangelists spare him the name Publican while he takes it himself, and answers pagan critics who called the following rash; the Gloss counts the call among the miracles and finds an omen in the crowd of sinners drawn after him.

positions.view: the word for sinners generally means heathens in the Gospels
no, since the Lord took care not to breach the Law by eating with Gentiles
Gentiles may have been present without the term designating them

outliers.claim: the brightness of the hidden Godhead in his face drew Matthew at first sight, as a loadstone draws iron

themes: And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.
And it came to pass, as Jesus sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples.

11.pericope_label: They that be whole need not a physician; I will have mercy, and not sacrifice

schools.summary: Barnes insists the prophetic saying is no repudiation of sacrifice but a Hebrew idiom preferring mercy, and explains that sacrifice stands for external religion at large; Ellicott reads grave irony in the proverb, hears the superiority of ethical to ceremonial law, and suspects the scribes were meant to read the prophet's context too.

Gill identifies go and learn as a rabbinic formula and takes the saying comparatively rather than absolutely; Calvin builds his longest passage on the scribes' two errors, calls the concession to their righteousness an admission made in irony, and turns the application on those who feel stained by communion with vile men.

Clarke turns the complaint inward on anyone who never felt himself indebted to mercy, preserves an older English rendering of mild-heartedness, and notes that the closing phrase about repentance was dropped from the text by Griesbach.
Chrysostom hears irony in the saying that he came not to call the righteous, since the text chooses mercy and rejects sacrifice rather than ranking them, and none on earth is righteous.

Rabanus develops the physician image, the healer wounded for our iniquities, the whole being those who establish their own righteousness; Augustine guards against supposing sinners loved because they are sinners; Hilary presses that no man is righteous by the law; the Gloss offers two senses of the righteous.

debates.question: Where does the quoted saying come from?

positions.view: Hosea
Samuel's rebuke of Saul

debates.question: Who are the righteous he did not come to call?

positions.view: the feignedly righteous who boasted of it
genuinely upright men such as Nathanael and the Baptist, needing no call to repentance

outliers.claim: attributes the words I will have mercy and not sacrifice to 1 Samuel rather than Hosea, against every other voice in the chapter

themes: And when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?
But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

14.pericope_label: Can the children of the bridechamber mourn while the bridegroom is with them?

schools.summary: Barnes and Robertson look to the Baptist's imprisonment as the occasion; Ellicott keeps his followers a distinct body with their own fasts and answers them without the sternness used on the Pharisees, denies the words impose an obligation while granting they sanction the principle, and marks the first plain hint of the death; Lightfoot traces the twice-weekly fast to a tradition of decrees of Ezra.

Calvin sees a stratagem to draw John's disciples into the Pharisees' party, warns that men are divided over trifles and outward rudiments, and will not object to deriving the bridegroom figure from the Baptist though he doubts it rests on solid grounds.
Clarke reports fasts undertaken to procure or avert dreams, and reconstructs a primitive annual fast commemorating the forty hours under death rather than forty days in the wilderness.
Henry observes that the boast was unverifiable, since Christ had told his disciples to keep their fasts private.

Chrysostom notices that the questioners name themselves before the Pharisees to add weight, and that Christ moves from calling himself Physician to calling himself Bridegroom, recalling the Baptist's own saying.

Augustine reconciles the three accounts by placing John's disciples among the other guests, and distinguishes two kinds of fasting answered separately here; Jerome reports a forty days' abstinence after Pentecost built on this text; Hilary reads the withdrawal as the loss of the food of life to those who do not believe Christ risen.

positions.view: the Baptist's disciples, as this Gospel says
the Pharisees brought them along, as they later brought the Herodians

debates.question: Do the words command later fasting?

positions.view: they sanction the principle without imposing an obligation, and favour occasional fasts over fixed ones

outliers.claim: calling the various primitive fasts a forty days' fast came of putting days where hours belonged

themes: Then came to him the disciples of John, saying, Why do we and the Pharisees fast oft, but thy disciples fast not?

And Jesus said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast.

16.pericope_label: New cloth on an old garment, and new wine into old bottles

schools.summary: Barnes and Robertson explain the unfulled cloth that shrinks and tears, and the skins that crack with age; Barnes reports a traveller's ox-skin bottle holding sixty gallons; Ellicott ties the three comparisons to the wedding, reads garment and wine as outer and inner life, and traces the same mistake through later church history.

Gill argues that the disciples, renewed by the Spirit, cannot be the old garments and old bottles, and holds with the reading that makes them the Scribes and Pharisees; Calvin says flatly that reading has no probability on its side, and answers that calling the disciples old means only that they wanted strength.
Clarke warns preachers that imposing mortifications before grace has prepared the heart is asking a child to do a man's work; Wesley glosses the harsher unwashed cloth.
Chrysostom takes the disciples as not yet renewed by the Spirit, and finds a standing instruction to receive converts from the whole world leniently.

Remigius identifies the new cloth with grace and the new wine with the fulness of the Spirit the disciples could not yet hold; Jerome makes the old garment the Scribes and Pharisees; the Gloss warns against loading the untrained; Hilary and Rabanus read the figures of the sacraments and of works and faith.

debates.question: What do the old garment and old skins stand for?

positions.view: the Scribes and Pharisees, who could not bear Gospel precepts
the weak disciples, not yet strong enough for a severe discipline

outliers.claim: the Church has repeated the same error, engrafting ordinances, vows and conventions on lives still barbarous or worldly

themes: No man putteth a piece of new cloth unto an old garment, for that which is put in to fill it up taketh from the garment, and the rent is made worse.
Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.

18.pericope_label: My daughter is even now dead: but come and lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live

schools.summary: Lightfoot and Ellicott define the ruler's office against the synagogue overseer's; Barnes, Clarke and Robertson resolve the apparent contradiction with the other Gospels grammatically, since the phrase need mean no more than that she must by now have died; Ellicott decides for this Gospel's order because its author was present.

Gill notes what Christ passed over in silence, the weakness of supposing he must come in person; Calvin refuses to make two stories of the accounts, likens their convergence to three fingers pointing at one object, and sets this ruler's faith beside the centurion's to its disadvantage.

Clarke distinguishes the two synagogue functionaries, reports a conjecture that an underlying Hebrew form could be pointed either way, and turns the rising to follow on ministers who should go to the bedside.
Henry answers the Gospel's own question whether any of the rulers believed by pointing to this one, whose faith condemned the rest.

Chrysostom stresses that the petitioner's rank embarrassed the Pharisees, calls the double request dullness, likening it to Naaman's expectation of the prophet, and notes that only three disciples went in.

Augustine answers the discrepancy by intention rather than idiom and draws the rule that we should attend to a speaker's meaning rather than his words; Remigius bids us imitate a mercy that rose the moment it was asked; Rabanus and Hilary read the ruler as Moses or as the Law itself.

debates.question: Was the girl already dead when the father spoke?

positions.view: the phrase need mean only that she must by now have died
he had so despaired that he asked for her recall to life, and this Gospel reports his mind rather than his words
a guess from the length of the journey, or a petitioner exaggerating his trouble
this Gospel's, since its author was present
the others leave room for an interval, into which the feast fits

outliers.claim: the heathen centurion showed the full brightness of faith and this officer of the synagogue scarcely a spark, yet Christ yields to his prayer

themes: While he spake these things unto them, behold, there came a certain ruler, and worshipped him, saying, My daughter is even now dead: but come and lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live.
And Jesus arose, and followed him, and so did his disciples.

20.pericope_label: If I may but touch his garment: thy faith hath made thee whole

schools.summary: Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson explain the fringe of the outer cloak, Ellicott reconstructing the whole dress and reporting that tradition fixed the number of its threads; Ellicott notes that her twelve years of hope deferred span the ruler's twelve years of joy, and Robertson concedes an element of superstition in her faith; Lightfoot invites the reader to judge the story of the statues for himself.

Gill argues that the touch could not defile Christ, whose power removed her impurity instead, and that the chief purpose of the turning was to steady Jairus; Calvin suspects a mixture of sin and error in her act, warns that imitators of remarkable examples without God's command are apes, and concludes that faith needs forgiveness to please God.

Clarke declines to describe the complaint, saying prudence forbids it, and glosses the word of dismissal as a call to courage; Wesley attributes her coming from behind to bashfulness and the legal uncleanness.
Chrysostom gives four reasons why she was not allowed to slip away unnoticed, among them the correcting of her supposing she could be hidden and the display of her faith for imitation.

Jerome observes that the Law shut her out of house and town so she met him on the road, and stresses the perfect tense of the healing word; Remigius contrasts the Lord's hem with the Pharisees' broad fringes; Rabanus reads her twelve years against the girl's; Hilary argues that taking a body did not confine a power no body can contain.

debates.question: Was her belief faith or superstition?

positions.view: faith mixed with sin and error, accepted but not to be copied
an element of superstition, honoured all the same
she believed the power but not the love, and the germ was accepted

debates.question: What of the statues said to have been set up by the healed woman?

positions.view: relayed as reported, with the name given her by an apocryphal gospel
the reader should weigh the narrative and judge what the story is worth

outliers.claim: outward things were endowed with a virtue not their own, as the handkerchiefs carried from Paul were

themes: And, behold, a woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind him, and touched the hem of his garment:
For she said within herself, If I may but touch his garment, I shall be whole.
But Jesus turned him about, and when he saw her, he said, Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made thee whole. And the woman was made whole from that hour.

23.pericope_label: The maid is not dead, but sleepeth: and they laughed him to scorn

schools.summary: Lightfoot cites the rule that even the poorest owed two pipes and a lamenting woman, and observes that calling death sleep was ordinary rabbinic idiom, which makes the form of Christ's speech worth weighing; Barnes catalogues the eastern expressions of grief and defends the small audience as five impartial witnesses; Robertson passes on the unsentimental account of why the crowd came.
Gill holds that the mockers were unworthy to be spectators, and that concealment became impossible once neighbours who had known her dead saw her walking and eating.

Clarke sets the Jewish practice beside an Irish lament he had watched himself, notes a decree restraining the drinking at wakes, and adds the Roman custom of calling the dead by name for eight days; Wesley distinguishes flutes for children from louder instruments for adults.

Chrysostom supposes the delay deliberate, so that the girl might actually die, and reads the derision as itself the proof of death, adding that food was ordered afterwards so the cure might not be thought a delusion.

Jerome applies the scene bitterly to teachers who are only minstrels singing dirges; Hilary makes the house the synagogue whose songs of the Law sounded a strain of wailing; Rabanus reads the girl as the soul dead in thought and the minstrels as flatterers.

debates.question: In what sense was she not dead but sleeping?

positions.view: not literally alive; the word affirms the body dead while implying the spirit lives, against a Sadducee opinion that she had ceased to be
a suspension rather than an end
reassurance and a lesson not to fear death, the departed soul being recalled rather than another introduced

outliers.claim: the exclamation covers the whole day's miracles, not this cure alone

themes: And when Jesus came into the ruler’s house, and saw the minstrels and the people making a noise,
He said unto them, Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth. And they laughed him to scorn.
But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose.
And the fame hereof went abroad into all that land.

27.pericope_label: Two blind men followed him: according to your faith be it unto you

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the touch as the first instance of a method used afterwards with the blind, explaining that men shut out from the Healer's face needed acts they could connect with the purpose to heal, and observes that the commentators divide on confessional lines over the disobedience; Robertson traces the verb of stern command through its use of snorting horses.

Gill and Calvin read the delay as a testing of constancy; Calvin cautions that knowledge of Christ's power is cold without persuasion of his willingness, draws the doctrine that prayer in faith is never refused, and calls the spreading of the report blameworthy while admitting the reason for the ban is unknown.
Clarke derives the verb of charging from a word meaning to roar or storm with anger, and insists the men should have held their peace, since to obey is better than sacrifice.
Henry contrasts men who believed on hearing alone with rulers who saw and denied, faith coming by hearing.

Chrysostom indicts those who watched the miracles and would not believe, gives three reasons for healing indoors, and holds that we should stop those who praise us for ourselves but promote what is said to the Lord's glory.

Jerome aims the title Son of David at heretics who mangle the Old Testament; Remigius explains why a man who knew asked the question, and reads the pair as the two nations; Gregory works out the paradox that good deeds should be hid by design and published under compulsion; Rabanus makes the house the heavenly Jerusalem.

debates.question: Were the men right to spread the report despite the charge?

positions.view: yes; what is said to the Lord’s glory should be promoted, and gratitude could not keep quiet
no; to obey is better than sacrifice, and their haste was blameworthy

outliers.claim: patristic and Roman Catholic commentators approve the disobedience while Protestant commentators do not, a division the chapter’s own voices reproduce exactly

themes: And when Jesus departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.
And when he was come into the house, the blind men came to him: and Jesus saith unto them, Believe ye that I am able to do this? They said unto him, Yea, Lord.
Then touched he their eyes, saying, According to your faith be it unto you.
And their eyes were opened; and Jesus straitly charged them, saying, See that no man know it.
But they, when they were departed, spread abroad his fame in all that country.

32.pericope_label: It was never so seen in Israel: he casteth out devils through the prince of the devils

schools.summary: Ellicott describes catalepsy or a sullen silence and insists the dumbness was spiritual rather than congenital, and sets the crowd's wonder deliberately against the Pharisees' aloofness; Robertson glosses the word as blunted and reads the charge as desperation; Lightfoot takes the exclamation to cover the whole day and reconstructs its sequence.

Gill notes how closely the prophecies were fulfilled; Calvin agrees the possessing spirit had taken the use of speech, calls the exclamation hyperbolical while allowing for the design of the sign, and warns that wickedness at the height of blindness will pervert any work of God.
Clarke explains that demons hid their work under the look of natural disorder, calls it consummate malice to ascribe God's works to the devil, and traces the charge to envy.
Henry observes that of the two a dumb devil is better than a blaspheming one, since nothing convinces those under the power of pride.
Chrysostom says the demon's malignity caused the affliction, so the man had to be brought and no faith was required of him, and calls the Pharisees' explanation foolish on its own terms.

Remigius admires the sequence of cures against the prophecy and reads the Gentiles as the dumb man; Augustine draws the rule that like events related separately by one evangelist are not the same event; Jerome divides the two responses; Hilary sees a world diseased in every part.

debates.question: How should near-identical narratives in different Gospels be treated?

positions.view: as like but not identical events, since one evangelist relates both at different points
the Lucan parallel would be taken for this one but for the answer attached there to a later miracle

outliers.claim: the saying that it was never so seen in Israel is hyperbolical, since greater miracles had been done among that people before

themes: As they went out, behold, they brought to him a dumb man possessed with a devil.
And when the devil was cast out, the dumb spake: and the multitudes marvelled, saying, It was never so seen in Israel.
But the Pharisees said, He casteth out devils through the prince of the devils.

35.pericope_label: Moved with compassion: the harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few

schools.summary: Ellicott treats the summary as a second Galilean circuit introducing the next chapter's discourse, prefers the reading that makes the crowd harried rather than merely faint, notes the first synoptic appearance of the harvest figure, and catches Christ asking his companions for fellowship in prayer; Barnes builds instead on the received reading and the pastoral scene; Robertson has the crowds rent as if by wild beasts.

Gill raises the question whether the Lord of the harvest is the Father or Christ himself; Calvin reads the summary as forestalling an objection, turns the shepherdless flock on idle priests and on the clergy of his own day, restricts the harvest to the elect, and makes prayer the only remedy for a scarcity of pastors.

Clarke traces the word for compassion to the bowels, reports that the rabbins were called reapers, and observes that those fittest for the work are usually most backward; Wesley notes that scribes were in every city but none cared for souls, and that the work is so full of reproach that nature may shrink from it.

Chrysostom finds the circuit itself an answer to the charge of collusion with demons, and hears Christ quietly claiming to be the Lord of the harvest, since the Apostles reap what he had sown through the Prophets.

Jerome notes that preaching came first and healing after, so works might convince those whom words would not; Remigius contrasts the good shepherd with the hireling and dates the increase of labourers to the seventy-two and to Pentecost; the Gloss separates long complaints from lesser infirmities.

positions.view: weary and burdened, like sheep straying without a shepherd
harassed and flayed, preyed on by wolves and thieves

debates.question: Who is the Lord of the harvest addressed in prayer?

positions.view: the Father
the Father or Christ himself, in which case prayer is offered to Christ

outliers.claim: feeling compassion is not enough for Christ, who craves the sympathy of his disciples and needs their fellowship in prayer

themes: And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease among the people.
But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
